blocks.x: A little extra breathing room in your bank account would go a long way in New York. For eligible workers and families, an IRS tax credit could help provide it.
According to the IRS’s official 2026 figures, the Earned Income Tax Credit, or EITC, is worth up to $8,231, depending on your income, filing status, and number of qualifying children.
Workers with one qualifying child could receive up to $4,427, while some workers without children can qualify, too.

Here’s the part worth knowing: you may be eligible even if you don’t owe federal income tax. The EITC is refundable, meaning it can reduce your tax bill and potentially put money back in your pocket through a refund, as the IRS explains.
These amounts apply to income earned in 2026 and are generally claimed on the return you file in 2027, rather than being automatic payments arriving now.
And for New Yorkers, the federal credit may only be part of the picture: New York State and New York City offer their own earned income credits for qualifying filers.
Here’s who could qualify, how much the credit is worth, and how a resulting refund could reach your bank account.
What is the Earned Income Tax Credit?
The Earned Income Tax Credit is a federal tax benefit for eligible people who work and earn a low to moderate income.
That can include employees and self-employed workers. You don’t have to be a parent, although the amount you can claim changes depending on whether you have qualifying children.

Unlike a deduction, which reduces the income you’re taxed on, a tax credit reduces the tax you owe dollar for dollar. A refundable credit can go further, potentially generating a refund after your tax liability reaches zero.
There is one step you can’t skip: filing.
According to the IRS’s EITC guidance, you must submit a tax return to claim the credit, even if you wouldn’t otherwise be required to file.
How much could you receive for 2026?
The IRS’s published maximum amounts for tax year 2026 are:
No qualifying children: up to $664.
One qualifying child: up to $4,427.
Two qualifying children: up to $7,316.
Three or more qualifying children: up to $8,231.
The $4,427 figure you may have seen making headlines applies specifically to eligible workers with one qualifying child. It isn’t the overall maximum or a flat payment available to everyone.
The key words are “up to.”
The credit increases with earnings over an initial range, reaches a maximum, and then gradually decreases as income rises.
Your final refund is a separate calculation, too. The credit may reduce taxes you owe or increase a refund, so the maximum credit amount shouldn’t be read as a guaranteed bank deposit.
What are the 2026 income limits?
Under the IRS’s 2026 rules, the federal EITC phases out completely when your adjusted gross income, or earned income if higher, reaches these amounts:
No qualifying children: $19,540 for eligible non-joint filers, or $26,820 for married couples filing jointly.
One qualifying child: $51,593 for eligible non-joint filers, or $58,863 for married couples filing jointly.
Two qualifying children: $58,629 for eligible non-joint filers, or $65,899 for married couples filing jointly.
Three or more qualifying children: $62,974 for eligible non-joint filers, or $70,244 for married couples filing jointly.
These are the points where the credit reaches zero, not the earnings levels that guarantee the largest credit.
Eligible non-joint filers include single and head-of-household filers. Married taxpayers who don’t file jointly must meet the IRS’s special separated-spouse requirements.
What other requirements do you need to meet?
Income is only one part of the check.
Under the IRS’s EITC eligibility rules, you generally must:
Have earned income from work, including qualifying wages, tips, or self-employment earnings.
Have valid Social Security numbers for yourself, your spouse if filing jointly, and any children claimed for the credit, issued by the return’s due date, including extensions.
Be a U.S. citizen or resident alien throughout the year, subject to a limited exception for certain joint filers.
Not file Form 2555 to claim the foreign earned income exclusion.
Meet the applicable filing-status and dependent rules.
Your investment income counted under EITC rules must also be no more than $12,200 for 2026.

Freelancers and gig workers shouldn’t assume they’re excluded. Qualifying self-employment earnings can count, but accurate income and expense records matter. The IRS’s EITC publication explains how earned income is calculated, including for self-employed taxpayers. Be sure to use the applicable 2026 instructions when filing your 2026 return.

Getty Images / NoDerog
Can you qualify without children?
Yes. You don’t need to be a parent to claim the EITC.
The maximum federal credit for eligible workers without qualifying children is $664 for 2026, subject to the lower income limits above.
Additional rules apply. Under the IRS’s eligibility guidance, you generally must:
Be at least 25 but under 65 at the end of the year.
Live in the United States for more than half the year.
Not be claimable as someone else’s dependent or qualifying child.
For married couples filing jointly, at least one spouse must meet the age requirement.
So, even if the larger family-credit amounts don’t apply to you, it may still be worth checking.
What counts as a qualifying child?
The IRS looks at relationship, age, residency, and joint-return requirements, not just whether someone appears as a dependent on your return.
According to the IRS’s qualifying-child rules, a child generally must live with you in the United States for more than half the tax year and meet one of these age conditions:
Be under 19 at year-end and younger than you, or your spouse if filing jointly.
Be under 24, a full-time student for at least five months of the year, and younger than you or your spouse.
Be any age if permanently and totally disabled.
Eligible relationships can include children, stepchildren, qualifying foster children, siblings, and descendants such as grandchildren, nieces, and nephews.

Shared custody or a multigenerational household can make this less straightforward. The same IRS guidance explains the tie-breaker rules that apply when more than one person could claim the same child.
New Yorkers could claim additional state and city credits
This is the part NYC residents shouldn’t overlook.

The New York State earned income credit is generally equal to 30% of your allowable federal EITC, reduced by any applicable household credit. It is fully refundable for full-year New York State residents, with different refundability rules for other filers.

Then there’s the separate New York City earned income credit. It ranges from 10% to 30% of your federal EITC, depending on your New York adjusted gross income. Eligible part-year city residents can also qualify, with an adjustment based on their residency period.
These credits are claimed through your New York State return. The state’s Form IT-215 instructions explain the claim process, but make sure you use the version for the tax year you’re filing.
Before signing your return, ask your software or preparer to check all three: federal, state, and city.
How do you claim the credit?
You claim the EITC through your tax return, rather than completing a separate application for a cash grant.
According to the IRS’s filing guidance, eligible taxpayers generally file Form 1040 or Form 1040-SR and attach Schedule EIC if claiming the credit with a qualifying child.
Tax software or the relevant IRS worksheets can help calculate the amount. For 2026 earnings, you’ll generally claim the credit during the 2027 filing season, using the 2026 forms and instructions.
When could the money reach your bank account?

Any resulting federal refund comes after you file and the IRS processes your return. Choosing direct deposit allows that refund to go into your bank account, but it does not turn the EITC into a separate automatic payment.

There’s also a timing rule to know. The IRS cannot issue refunds on returns claiming the EITC before mid-February. That restriction applies to the entire federal refund, not just the part linked to this credit.
For 2026 returns filed in 2027, that means you should not expect an EITC-related refund before mid-February 2027. It isn’t a guaranteed arrival date, either.

Filing time, processing, additional reviews, and your bank can affect when the money becomes available. Check the IRS’s EITC refund guidance for the relevant filing season rather than relying on a payment date quoted for an earlier year.
For now, keep your earnings records together and put this on your filing checklist. You don’t have to owe federal income tax to benefit, but you do have to file and claim what you’re eligible for.
